title: Week 3: Transitioning to Scenario Intelligence
text: At the end of week two, the phase three prototype had been reviewed, its limitations documented, and the need for a scenario-based decision intelligence layer established. The next step was to design that layer before implementing it. During this period, I focused on how Causal Couture could move beyond displaying current business signals and support structured what-if analysis for fashion inventory and demand decisions. title: The Four Adjustable Scenario Variables
text: Users modify selected business assumptions and examine how the existing analytical signals and recommendations would respond. The initial design centered on four adjustable variables: demand change, inventory change, engagement change, and conversion change. Together, they define the first set of assumptions a user could explore. Every scenario would begin with the current

title: Baseline vs. Scenario: Side-by-Side Recalculations
text: Baseline and the user's hypothetical assumptions. Those assumptions would then pass into the analytical workflow to produce recalculated scenario signals. The resulting view would show differences between the baseline and scenario, the direction of change, a resulting recommendation, an explanation, and the confidence or context information needed to interpret it. This structure was designed to keep the current business state visible while placing the hypothetical state beside it.

title: Defensive Engineering: Setting Scenario Validation Boundaries
text: The user could compare what changed without confusing the simulation with observed business performance. For example, a user could increase the demand assumption while decreasing available inventory. The scenario view could then show whether the stock risk and recommendation signals became more urgent under those assumptions. This is controlled what-if simulation, not forecasting. text: Hypothetical situation is likely to occur. It is also not causal inference and does not claim that one variable produced another. The proposed layer would initially use the existing heuristic analytical framework. Its purpose was to recalculate decision support signals under controlled assumptions, not to predict the future or establish causal effects. I also planned validation boundaries for

title: Designing a Modular Backend Architecture
text: Scenario inputs. Unrealistic or malformed assumptions would need to be controlled before they entered the analytical workflow and affected the simulated result. The front end also needed a clearer structure. I planned five primary sections: overview, data, intelligence, scenario lab, and insights. The intended journey became upload, validate, integrate, analyze, simulate, and decide. Scenario lab was planned as the future interactive space for modifying assumptions and comparing the baseline business state with a simulated state before moving toward a decision. The wider UX plan included clearer functional separation, KPI presentation, structured recommendation cards, source availability indicators, progressive disclosure, sticky navigation, responsive layouts, system feedback, improved hierarchy, and a stronger fashion-oriented visual identity. Scenario intelligence also required a more modular back end. I outlined separate responsibilities for core scorecard calculations, scenario simulation, trend analysis, alert generation, and dashboard aggregation. This separation would allow the same analytical calculations to support both the baseline dashboard and future scenario analysis. The logic could be reused across both workflows instead of being duplicated. By the end of week three, the scenario intelligence framework, its inputs and outputs, methodological boundaries, scenario lab experience, and modular back end architecture had been designed and prepared for implementation.
